title: 5. IP Routing and Forwarding
content: #### **Forwarding vs Routing** **Forwarding**: Selecting an output port based on destination address and routing table. A data-plane action. - A *forwarding table* is used when a packet is being forwarded. A row contains the mapping from a network number to an outgoing interface and some MAC information, such as Ethernet Address of the next hop. **Routing**: The process by which a routing table is built. This is computing paths the packets will follow. A control-plane action. - *Routing table* used by the routing algorithm as a *precursor* to build the forwarding table. A mapping of network number to next hop. **Hop-by-Hop Packet Forwarding**: Router receives a packet. It then: 1. Inspects destination IP address 2. Indexes into the table 3. Determines the outgoing interface 4. Forwards the packet out that interface # Routing Algorithms Problem can be viewed as finding the lowest cost path between any two nodes. But this is much harder than a basic graph problem because networks are not static: - Node or links can fail - New nodes or links can be added - The cost of an edge can change ## Naive Flooding Routers forward packets to all ports except the ingress port. Although simple, it is inefficient as routers can receive the same packet multiple times and loops are possible. ## Distance Vector (Bellman-Ford) *An iterative, asynchronous and distributed version of Bellman-Ford.* Each node constructs a 1D array containing the "distances" to all other nodes and distributes that vector to its immediate neighbours. - Assumes that a node knows the cost of the link to each of its directly connected neighbours Every $T$ seconds each router sends its table to its neighbour, each router then updates its table based on the new information. When a node detects a link failure, it will set the distance to $\infty$ and send an update to it's neighbours. ### Count to Infinity Problem Under the wrong sequence of table updates, we could run into the **count-to-infinity** problem. A cycle where the distance to reach a node after a link failures keeps increasing up until $\infty$ that will only be detected once an abnormally high number is reached. - We can use some relatively small number as an approximation of infinity. **Split-Horizon**: Don't send include the routes learned from a neighbour in table updates. - **Split-Horizon with Poison Reverse**: When negative information (setting count to infinity) is included in the table updates for rows where the route was learned from a neighbour. Done to ensure that the neighbour will never use the information it provided to derive it's own path. ## Link State Routing Send to all nodes information about directly connected links using **Link State Packets (LSP)**. - LSPs contain the id of the node and the cost each link to directly connected neighbours of said node. They include a sequence number and a TTL. We can use LSPs to do reliable flooding because we can discard packets when $TTL = 0$ and use the $SEQNO$ to differentiate link updates. Use Dijkstra's algorithm where the graph is formed from all the LSPs a node has received so far. - Maintains two lists tentative and confirmed but tentative can essentially viewed as the heap within Dijkstras
